Mr. Speaker, in echoing the words of the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) I want to point out again that the spirit of parliamentary reform is what we should be concerning ourselves with. It was in that spirit that earlier today Madam Speaker-even though there might have been a difference of opinion with respect to interpreting the rules or the words of the Standing Order on the experimental rules-pointed out that it is in the interest of fairness and justice that she reserve judgment and take into consideration the intent and purpose of parliamentary reform.
Parliament and parliamentarians have fallen into disrepute. They lack the respect and confidence of the people of this country. In the eyes of the news media we are losing credibility. That is why parliamentary reform had to come, Mr. Speaker. I cannot help but say, as Madam Speaker pointed out this morning, that we have to keep in mind the purpose and intent of the reform which the general public of Canada rejoiced over when they heard that at last this House was introducing the reform for which they have waited so long. When that reform package was introduced, the stated purpose was that it would enable this democratic assembly to operate more fairly and effectively. It was designed to protect the rights of Members of the House, not only Members of the Government but of Members of the Opposition.
There was a consensus that the time of Parliament could be better organized and made more productive. The search was on to find ways to enable private Members to make a greater input to legislation and to the productivity of the House. More free votes were to be called and developed for private Members.
I suggest that the public at large is not aware of the ineffectiveness of the committee system in years gone by. The Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) and the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid) and others turned their attention to the broad subject of parliamentary reform, but still other Members were looking to the committee system as a means of providing individuals with a greater opportunity to add to the productivity of the House.
Each of us was elected in a democratic way to represent a sizeable segment of the population of the country. It is that individual Member who is the cornerstone of the parliamentary system. It is in the interests of the country that the highest calibre of person be attracted to become a Member of Parliament. It should follow that Members of Parliament be given an opportunity to make a meaningful contribution to the consideration, deliberation and development of legislation. That has not been the practice in the past, however.
There was a broad consensus that the committee system was not effective, and that is putting the matter kindly. There was a wide range of variance in the volume of work that the committees had to consider. Reference has been made to that today. There were regional differences, and the frequency of meetings and a number of other things contributed to a discrepancy between one standing committee and another.
When the third report of the Standing Committee was introduced, not too much concern was expressed about the provision that the standing committees be composed of not less than 10 and not more than 15 Members. It was viewed as a range within which the Striking Committee would operate and within which the number of parliamentarians to serve on the respective committees would be determined.
I was rather disturbed when the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans), who is a member of the Striking Committee, spoke of altering the range and making it from

nine to 17 members. Why was that not done before and, as it was not done before, why does the NDP not introduce an amendment now to correct that injustice-an injustice which obviously prevailed and which, as the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain pointed out, the Striking Committee report invokes upon Members of the Progressive Conservative Party?
As the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River pointed out, the Striking Committee gave additional powers to committees. When there was some comment with respect to the capacity of the chairmen, however, the Hon. Member for London East (Mr. Turner) pointed out that the chairman has to be picked from the Government side. There were additional comments to the effect that there has to be a cushion of Members. The chairman is protected from breaking a tie vote but there has to be a cushion of Government Members, six, three and one, on all committees except two. I cannot think of anything more unfair than that.
As we start off on a basis of parliamentary reform we start off on a basis of unfairness that puts 37 Members on this side of the House in the position of not being able to serve their riding or being able to do the job they want to do in the House. They are deliberately prevented from so doing by Hon. Members opposite who abuse the right of the majority.
The good beginning made by parliamentary reform will be negated by this third report if it is carried today, as I presume it will be.
I do not want to abuse the time of the House, Mr. Speaker, but I should like to make one personal reference. The Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River emphasized the necessity of developing a specialty. Then the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Smith) emphasized that it was not a good thing to have a chairman who must break a tie. Like myself, that Member served on municipal Government and sat on committees. He watched his mayor break ties. That was his responsibility. If he was a man at all, that was his job. I see no reason why the Government should protect its chairman from the necessity of breaking a tie. I think it is an abuse of the system to say that there must be a majority of Government Members to provide a cushion, notwithstanding the chairman. To say that the chairman does not reflect the attitude of the Government is completely wrong.
Parliamentary Secretaries sit in to echo the comments of their Minister, if the Minister is not present. These are passed on to the chairman, and the chairman is a reflection of the wants and wishes of the Minister.
I was the mayor of a municipality and we had to make decisions and break tie votes. I was the mayor of an urban industrial city of 125,000 people. I am not now in a position to reflect the attitudes of that automotively oriented city. I am not now in a position to reflect the concerns of the marine industry which is developing along the Welland Canal. As a veteran with perhaps the longest service of any Member of this House-five years and eight months-am I in a position to sit as a Member of the Veterans' Committee?
Striking Committee Report
I consider the actions of the Striking Committee and of the majority of Members on the Government side in limiting the membership of committees to be a devious means of preventing Members of the Opposition from speaking out. It is a means of cutting down on the opportunities of Members to serve their constituencies. Members of the Government have looked after themselves. The Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River made a plausible argument. He said, "We are affected too". But I have already pointed out that there are 37 Conservative Members who are not able to sit on a committee because of the Striking Committee report. Does it affect the other side? There is provision for 120 members as opposed to 64, which is not proportionate to the representation in the House, or opportunities for Members to sit on committees. They appoint the representatives from the Speaker's chair down. They have the Cabinet and the Parliamentary Secretaries. No wonder they are not concerned with or interested in a change of the membership of committees. They do not have the bodies to put in them. They are all fixed with a second opportunity to serve, already. Where is the equity and fairness in that kind of situation as it applies to this side of the House?
The Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain said that he recognized the unfairness. It is there, but to adopt or support the amendment would give an opportunity to put 20 more of the unemployed 37 Members of the House to work. He indicated that it would sort of give a greater disadvantage to their side because it would not be proportionately the same. The Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain is on the Striking Committee. I do not know, because I was not privy to the actions which took place, but I heard the Government Whip, the Hon. Member for London East, point out that he voted with the Government to introduce the report and that he voted in support of it.
What is the position of the New Democratic Party? What amendments does it propose to bring forward? I heard the rhetoric and the comments with respect to a neutral chairman. I heard that the NDP would not support the amendment which my colleague proposed to bring forward, but I have not heard of any NDP amendment to the report which is unfair to us, as the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain now recognizes, and to them as it presently exists. Surely there is a better way of improving the situation. Surely there is an opportunity for the House to start off parliamentary reform on the basis of equity. If we miss the opportunity today, then it might not come around again.
The Government side fails to appreciate that even though these are experimental rules for one year, the possibility is that precedents are being made. I rejoice in the precedent established by Her Honour Madam Speaker this morning. I rejoice in it because it was a precedent with which she was concerned, but this will be a dangerous precedent if it is followed. Also, Government Members fail to recognize that they do not rule by the divine right of kings. The opportunity will soon come when they will be replaced. If they adopt this as a precedent

Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to speak too long because my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid), answered most of the criticisms of the Opposition in a very good speech a few moments ago. I think we have to emphasize what both of us are trying to achieve, at least on the Government side. I remind Hon. Members opposite that just because we sit on this side does not mean that we are of the Government. We are supporters of the Government, and we certainly have our own independent judgments. While we may support the Government, it does not mean to say that we always agree with the Government on every issue.
I would count the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River and myself as two of the leading proponents. We are trying to convince the Government, and hopefully the Opposition, to try to shift the emphasis in Parliament so that the criticisms which were made by Professor Lower in the article which he wrote in a recent edition of Macleans, to which the Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) referred, can be realized. Professor Lower made some very good points about the diminishing effectiveness of Parliament. He really laid it at the feet of Members of Parliament themselves and their attitudes. He indicated that it did not matter what institutional or structural changes there were in the House, that unless the attidues were changed, the House would not be improved. I agree with that. Some of us are trying-and I am sure it is not only those of us on the Government side; I know that some of my colleagues on the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure are trying as well-to change the attitude certainly of the Government and also of the entrenched interests in the Opposition Parties. In effect, we are trying to change the attitudes of the Party leadership in the House-and it is not only that of the Government but that of the Party leadership of the Conservative Party and of the Party leadership of the New Democratic Party-to accept a more flexible system, one which gives more
independence to the role of Members of Parliament. We hope to achieve this through the committee system.
I would like to view this in terms of steps. We introduced the fourth report of the Committee, which has really been gathering dust. It received some comment, but it did not really come to much. It concerned the whole question of the method of selection of the Speakership. I do not propose to go into the substance of that issue, but it was a unanimous report which indicated that to try to do away with any inference that the Chair may be something less than impartial, we as Members should have a say in the selection of the Speaker. Also it indicated that it should not just rest with the Governor in Council, which in effect is the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). As tradition has developed within our system, it has become the Prime Minister's full prerogative. With all due respect to the current Prime Minister and previous ones, we believe that the decision-making process should be opened up and in fact returned to where it was. If we look back to our heritage in the British parliamentary system, the Speaker was reluctantly dragged to the chair by Members on all sides. It was not a calling from the Prime Minister of the day; they did not have prime ministers in those times. It was a collective decision of Members of the House that that person act as the Speaker. We have brought forth this idea in our fourth report. I am not saying it cannot be refined and I am not saying it does not have weaknesses. But if we can develop the notion of complete impartiality of the Chair, and I am not faulting you, Mr. Speaker, nor any of your colleagues in the Chair, and put aside any shadow of a doubt that the Chair is somewhat less than impartial, then I think we have a start in reforming this place.
The next step is to do what is done in Great Britain, and that is, to allow the Speaker to select committee chairmen, as mentioned by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River, according to seniority and competence so that the best people, the most impartial people, determined by the most impartial person in the House, the Speaker of the House, preside over our committees.
I would like to work toward that end. I hear a few cheers from the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) and the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Smith). I think we would like to work toward this end. Then it does not bother me as a supporter of one political Party, in this case the Government, that we have Opposition chairmen. When was the last time we heard criticism about the conduct of the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts, the Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke)? He has not been criticized. A tradition has grown up in this House that the Chairman of that Committee should be a Member of the Official Opposition. If that procedure can work in the Standing Committee on Public Accounts and in the Standing Committee on Management and Member's Services, surely it can work in all other committees. There should be more of an even balance.

Let me get to the point of the debate, the Striking Committee. Some of us made recommendations to the Government House leader. I want to take some of the heat off the Government here because some of us who are not Parliamentary Secretaries, gave our advice and said to him, "Look, if we are trying to develop this and if we are trying to make this approach of more independence work, not only for the Speaker but for the chairmen of the respective committees, then we believe that we should have a ratio in the committees so that the chairman is never forced to break a tie."
Earlier, the Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer) used the analogy of the Speaker and said that situation has never happened here, and if it does the rules are plain. But it will happen on every single item because of the ratio, if we accept the amendment put forward by the Hon. Member for Halifax West, of six, four and one. In the House of Commons we have 282 Members and we have the Government with a reasonable majority. It is not likely in this Parliament, and it has never happened to my knowledge, that the Speaker has had to break a tie vote. But in a committee made up of 11 Members, as suggested by the Hon. Member for Halifax West, it will mean that on every single item on procedural and on substantive matters the chairman will be forced to vote to break a tie. Until we change the attitude of the Party leadership, both on this side and certainly on the other side, in a majority Parliament a chairman will be from the Government benches. Therefore, that chairman will be forced into supporting the Government line. This will undermine the very thing we are trying to achieve. That is why I cannot understand the logic this afternoon of some Members on the other side. I hope this is just one further step in moving toward the development of a panel of chairmen.
I am glad members of the committee were able to travel to England early in January to see how things were there and to see that a coterie of highly respected, independently minded Members from all Parties has developed. These people have the confidence of all other Members in the House in running the House on an ongoing basis. That is what we want to achieve.
I had some experience on this matter stemming from the bell ringing incident last year. Luckily, I was away at the time. As punishment for being away at the time, I think the Government wanted me to be Chairman of the Special Energy Legislation Committee that was set up as a compromise following the bell ringing episode. I took on the chairmanship. But the membership split on that Committee was six, three and one. Who suggested that split of six, three and one? It was the Hon. Member for the Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), the Leader of the Opposition and former House leader of the Official Opposition. He was the gentleman who agreed to the compromise that ended the bell ringing incident breaking the omnibus Bill into eight separate Bills, and it was he who had those Bills referred to the special committee whose mandate has since expired.
It is somewhat odd that I was accused, not only by the Conservative Party but by my own colleagues, of being in

Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) accused me a number of times of protecting the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, now the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). Members on my own side came to me afterwards and said, "My God, you are letting those Tories run the committee."

I must admit it affected my judgment and my thinking on the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure in putting forward the notion of ten Members. Not everybody bought the idea of ten Members and we could not agree among ourselves, but we did agree that the membership should be reduced. We said, "All right, we do not want our lack of agreement on this one issue to spoil a unanimous report. Let us agree on the parameters of 10 Members and 15 Members for the committees and let us throw the actual numbering back to the House leaders."
I do not find it unusual that there is an impasse and that the Government has to force the issue. It is done all the time. This place does not operate with unanimity. It should not. It would be a very sterile place if it did. Every week the Opposition does not get its way, nor does the Government get its way, and where a compromise cannot be reached then someone has to take the initiative. Invariably the Government House leader will say, "I am sorry, you cannot agree on this, but we have to discharge our obligations to the House to get our package of legislation through and we will force the issue. We are responsible for the administration of business." The Government House leader says that such and such a day will be an allotted day. He tells us what business will be brought forward. He tells us when the Government will limit debate with time allocation, which I believe is now done by Standing Order 80. The Government House leader says when he will bring in closure. That is accepted in the parliamentary system. The fact that we could not unanimously agree on this particular point, or the fact that we could not agree, detracts somewhat from the spirit that was achieved by our committee and I think is really an argument we should put to rest.
I was bothered somewhat earlier by the comments made by some Members of the House, both on and off the Committee.

February 11, 1983
Striking Committee Report
Perhaps I attribute this to myself, that if we cannot agree on this we will not really go anywhere in terms of more procedural reform in the House. I hope that kind of childish argument, which is not confined to one corner of the House, will not gain any credence. The fact is that, at an impasse, the Government sought a compromise. There was somewhat of a compromise put forward by the NDP. I believe the NDP proposed as a compromise a membership made up of eight, five and two on the Standing Committee on Agriculture, and on the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence. I think it is a testimony to the Government that it has accepted the advice of backbenchers on its own side that we should accept a membership made up of ten Members. This will give people like myself more encouragement to press the Government further in developing the consent of a panel of chairmen from which a chairman could be chosen by the Speaker on the basis of merit. This panel could be composed of Members from both sides of the House. I am encouraged by the Government's acceptance to study this issue.
1 hope this debate will not sway us away from our responsibility as Members to make this institution a better place. The experience of the Committee up to this time has been good. I believe there has been some degree of satisfaction from all sides in our third report. Perhaps improvements can be made, but I hope they can be discussed.
I can understand especially the Conservatives' position since there are only 70 committee slots presently available and they have 102 Members. Therefore, many of their Members will not be full time Members of a particular committee. However, do we as Members have the right to expect to be on a committee, regardless of any consideration? I believe Members must earn their way around here. I include Government Members because some of us cannot be on committees either. The Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River is not happy with our Whip's committee choices in some cases. He will have to prove that our Whip was wrong and that he should be back on a particular committee. As well, Members of the Conservative Party will have to work hard to prove that they deserve a place on a committee.
I was concerned by the decision made in the Standing Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure to split up the committees. I believe that the 15-man committee for the Agriculture Committee is particularly unfair to Members of the Conservative Party, which draws many of its Members from western Canada who are concerned with agricultural matters. I would rather have seen two agriculture committees set up, perhaps similar to the British operation which has two agriculture committees. Perhaps one committee could study Canagrex-I hate to offend the Official Opposition with that word-and another one could study a farm support Bill. I believe two agriculture committees could deal with the problem.
I would also propose splitting the External Affairs and National Defence Committee into two separate committees. I
was a regular member of that Committee and I am now an alternate. 1 would like to have been a full time member of that committee. This could have been achieved if we had two ten-member committees, one for External Affairs and one for National Defence.
The Committee on Standing Orders and Procedures decided that this question will require more thought. We decided to defer that issue. This debate illustrates that the Committee will have to consider the matter seriously and urgently and come back to the House so that we may have more committees, which will enable Members on both sides to participate more fully in those committees. However, no one has the right to expect to sit on a committee automatically.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a short comment. The general impression that I am given from listening to the debate is that we are advancing greatly with regard to committee work. I admit that there has been some advance made, but I certainly do not see any great advance because the speech given by the Hon. While it may be utopian philosophy or hope, I do not believe it should matter if a Member is Liberal, Conservative, New Democratic or Independent when dealing with a subject such as agriculture. The agricultural problem certainly must be met and the solutions do not have to rest on the particular philosophy of any one Party. That is the weakness I see in the setting up of these committees. The Government will always have its way unless Government Members are persuaded otherwise. It is difficult to change the judgment of someone who is making up his mind that he will support the Government regardless of what happens. It is difficult for the Government to persuade the Opposition if the Opposition Members make up their minds that they will do whatever their Party wants. I do not see any great advance in this at all.
I am also concerned about the fact that my Province may not even be represented on some committees. At the present time, the Government has no representation in the House from Saskatchewan, Alberta or British Columbia. Consequently, we may not even have a voice in numerous committees. The people of Alberta have a right and expect to be heard in the committees, the same as people from any other Province. That is another area of concern.
February 11, 1983

If we do have the situation where Members are chosen for committees by the Speaker, as suggested by the Hon. Member, I hope they will not be chosen according to the criteria of that person. I believe we are sent here to represent the people who elected us, and that is what we should be doing in the House and in the committees, regardless of Party politics.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN THIRD REPORT OF STRIKING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say that I am not at all surprised that we have had unanimity in the House of Commons on parliamentary reform. Certainly, anyone who watches us on television would agree that we do need parliamentary reform. I believe that view is unanimous among all Members and all Canadians.
The question we must ask is, do we in fact have parliamentary reform or do we have something that looks like parliamentary reform but is merely tinkering that is ineffectual? Has the Government done this so it can say how productive it has been in achieving parliamentary reform?
I do not see much reform in this at all. It may be more regressive than progressive if the intent of this effort is not pure. I would like to think that the Government's intent is pure.
I enjoyed the idealism expressed by the Member for York East (Mr. Collenette) and the Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid). If we are to get what they said, then I am not so concerned. However, since I do not think that is the case, I am concerned. If those Hon. Members believe it, 1 do not think that they have been around long enough to see the reality of how this place works. I hope they were correct, because there is a great difference between parliamentary reform and efficiency and expediency which detracts from the parliamentary process.
I suggest that this report will do one of two things: either limit the powers of Parliament or extend them. I do not see anything about extension. I see the words, "the committee wishes to ensure limiting the number of Members". It is limitation. We brought forth an amendment which calls for the extension, a slight extension, a slight increase. But no, the Government says, "We cannot accept that". It wants to limit again. I am concerned about this word "limiting", and concerned about the rhetoric and reality of what could be an excercise and abuse of power, because there really is no power being exchanged here.
Surely we are trying to increase the capacity of this democracy in which we are participating to act more effectively. We are trying to make committees more relevant and flexible to respond to changes. However, I want to know how the External Affairs Committee is, for example, more flexible, more responsive to change, more capable of acting. I want to know how my role as a Member of Parliament is enhanced, let alone whether consideration has been given to the many Members who were cut off from the External Affairs Committee, Members who have been attending regularly and participating in so many different ways.
Striking Committee Report
I see the role of the External Affairs Committee changing daily. As a result of the Government prerogative in expanding Government positions, the ministry of External Affairs has now become a super ministry, and the Department of External Affairs is not just concerned with External Affairs. The Committee is now concerned with Defence, Cl DA, and now Trade is added to it. We have a much larger responsibility and we are cutting our membership way down.
I am really disappointed that the Hon. Member for York East was not able to get the Committee split. That would have been a start. Not only do we need to have the Committee split, but perhaps it should be split into three. Perhaps, for example, the Trade section could be added or maybe a special section for International Development. It just boggles the mind when one sees the functions of that Committee equated with those of the Committee on Management and Members' services, so that the two are supposedly equal committees, with equivalent power, authority and so forth.
I am greatly concerned about the intent of the Government. The intent of the Government to my way of thinking, is registered by what it thinks about committees as they relate to money and ability to legislate. That is what we do here. We legislate and we spend money. We collect money, we spend money and, hopefully, we even save money sometimes. However, the committees have really no capacity to do any of these things. They really only have the capacity to hear and to recommend. I am concerned about that fact, and I am also concerned that there is not a provision for extra staffing. It is stated that they can call staff, but I see no budgetary provision or anticipation by the Government that committees shall in fact be more effective through the capacity of their staff and that they will have the funds to accomplish their work. The Government intent is suspect, right there.
I have not heard any discussion today about making these committees more accessible to the Canadian public to ensure that the public can and will in fact be heard, that the committees will travel, they will be heard, their expenses will be paid, and this type of thing. I have not heard an expression of that spirit of reform. I hear some very broad principles enunciated, but there is no spirit of reform as such.
I have been in other parliamentary jurisdictions in Canada which have enjoyed the same privileges we are granting today. However, what happened was that although there could be an automatic reference made to a committee, the automatic reference would never be made. The committee would meet one day, elect its chairman, and have a majority but would never meet again for the rest of the session. It is one thing to have a reference, but quite another to ensure that committees meet. Will they meet regularly, automatically and in good faith? We have to accept that on the strength of intent and hope, and I do not see that, because I see words like "limit" creeping in everywhere.
The Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River said that the Committee wanted to enhance the role of the Private Member. I do not know how this enhances the role of 37 Hon. Members on this side who are now no longer permanent committee

February 11, 1983
Striking Committee Report
members. I feel that it detracts from their role as Members of Parliament and from their capacity to act. I do not see any enhancement there.
The Hon. Member said that, independent from the structure of the Party hierarchy, the Whips will have less power. The Whips have more power. In fact, the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River just finished indicating that he was not happy with what his Whip had done to him because he lost his position on several committees. The Whip does not have less power, the Whip has more power. He has more power to choose because he has more people from which to choose for more seats. Instead, we will find out that it will be back to the old tradition, with the Whips appointing the ones who keep their seats the warmest, not necessarily the ones out working in External Affairs and other areas, or those who put in extra energy, and sometimes the two go together but not necessarily.
The Hon. Member also said that private Members do not want authority. Private Members do want authority, but is this accomplished? What authority have they gained? What power have I gained as a private Member? I do not see any power that I have gained as a Private Member. I see limitations, but I see no power, because there has been no power transferred, only the ability to hear and make recommendations. There is no power to legislate or real power to control money. We saw the Estimates taken out of the House of Commons, and we thought it was great and we would have more to discuss. The Estimates are a farce. The House has no control and the committee has no control over spending. It did not work. It was a nice intention, but I am afraid that will happen here, too.
This report, if adopted, will also eliminate opportunity for the newcomer. Some people have been on this side of the House for ten years but they will not sit on a committee because the cuts are 37 deep. They are no longer on committee. How can one call what happened to other persons "opportunity"? I know of one Hon. Member who came here ten years ago with some hope, but he cannot even sit on a committee now. It is absolutely disgusting to see what is being done, at least what I think is being done.
There is no authority and no power. There is only pretence. There is a pretence at democracy rather than the practice of democracy. I am very concerned that the right of private Members to act is not being enhanced here. It will depend on the intent of the Government, but every time one passes power on to the Government, one gives up the authority of the House of Commons. Authority of the House of Commons is perhaps being transferred somewhat, but that transfer may result in reduced authority, not increased authority.
The proof will be in the eating, but I think we are being had here. Let us remember that this is a one year process. This is not even necessarily a precedent, because the whole matter will be reviewed in one year. Let us have that clearly understood. One year from now, if I have not experienced more authority as a Member of the Opposition, as a private Member, and if these 37 other Hon. Members have not somehow found ways to express themselves, ways which have now been cut off, then
maybe we had better look to a revision and the continuation of past practice.
Does the Government really mean what it is talking about, this reform? Will it continue with the next stage and the stage after that, or will this be it, in reality? That reality will be tested, as will the intent of the Government. I remain skeptical and doubtful, especially when the Government will not accept a simple amendment which is brought forward in good faith and which would permit a few more of our Members, not 37 Members, to have some small role to play. I cannot understand why the Government will not accept a little compromise so that a few more Hon. Members can have that right. The Government would maintain its control. It has its control because there are so few Hon. Members who are supposedly fighting for these positions. The Government does not have to worry about its quorum. They will be there now. They have to fight for their positions.

numbers correct but that the same basic structure of numbers is being maintained under the new system as was the case under the old system. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not saying that I am objecting to the Government having a majority. We have made a recommendation that we need to have at least one more member. named as members on that committee who will normally speak first who will prevent another Opposition member from speaking.
I think it is specious to say that there might be no one from Alberta on the Agriculture Committee and that an Alberta Member cannot participate. That is demonstrably untrue. It does not work that way today.
Another thing that I would like to point out, as other Members have noted, is that I have been around here a little while too, and I am one of those who participate in committee work, and I found precisely the opposite tendency. When something is hot, it is a really hot topic, there is a great deal of pressure in being a member of such a committee. At other times a committee cannot meet because it lacks a quorum. As a matter of fact, I have seen times when a committee is first struck when one of the first motions we pass to hear witnesses is passed without a quorum, because frequently we lack the necessary attendance. It is not that we lack opportunities to speak. Sometimes we have a workload that is so heavy, especially at certain periods of the year, that we cannot manage to attend committees and get all the things done that we are supposed to get done.
I would suggest to you that if we followed the British practice, we would not be concerned, as was the Member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid), with unemployed MPs running around with nothing to do and not attached to any committees. If one follows the British practice, a set of committees can be developed which are select committees. In the British House of Commons they have seven domestic committees, including the Committee on Privileges; they have three legislative committees that deal with everything from the European Common Market to the consolidation of Bills. Then they have the oversights of Government, which are called select committees but are really standing committees. But if we move to select committees to treat legislation, or legislative committees, and continue on with our departmentally oriented standing committees, plus our task forces, I am quite certain there would be more than enough for all of us to do.
Speaking of the task forces, I think they did a remarkable job. I would like to see some arrangement where the House, as someone else has said, could direct a task force to begin its work. committees on Estimates, if you like, from the legislative committees, which could be just temporary committees. Mr. Speaker, in listening to the final remarks of the Hon. Member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. Rose), I cannot help but wonder what the magic is in waiting a year for democracy to be restored to this House. We are witnessing a situation where the Government has given itself 50 per cent more Members on a committee than the Opposition, and we see a degree of complicity by the New Democratic Party, who will not support the amendment before the House, which would refer this matter back to the Striking Committee to ensure that fairness and equity is exercised in the determination of committee sizes. Why, Mr. Speaker? Let us look at the actual breakdown of proportional representation on the committee of ten which has been proposed. The NDP would have one member, giving them 10 per cent, the Official Opposition would have three members, giving us 30 per cent, and the Government would have 60 per cent of the representation on that committee. The NDP, Mr. Speaker, is getting proportionately a better deal than the Official Opposition because in fact we have 36 per cent of the seats in this House but we are only being given 30 per cent of the positions on committee. That is the beginning of the injustice, Mr. Speaker, and only the beginning. If we look at the proportional representations, the number of seats the NDP have in this House, we will find it represents 11 per cent of the total. And yet it is getting 10 per cent. If you look at the ratio, you will find, Mr. Speaker, that on a proportional basis, this Party is being hit more drastically than the NDP, because if you take the two 15 member committees being established, the NDP has 13.3 of its representation on those committees, and this Party has only 33 per cent. So the NDP have a good deal going for them. That is why they are guilty of complicity with the Government in this matter and are prepared to wait a whole year, while Members of the Official Opposition are deprived of their right to represent the concerns of their constituents before the standing committees of this House.
The basic injustice which has been presented this afternoon is that every Member of the Government will sit on a committee or in Cabinet, or carry the title of Parliamentary Secretary. Indeed, there will be 124 positions created for Government
Striking Committee Report
Members on committees. There will be doubling up in some cases. And every backbench Member of the Libera! Party will be able to go home wearing on his sleeve at least a representation on one committee of this House, whereas 40 per cent of the Members of the Official Opposition will not be given an opportunity to represent the particular interests which they bring to this place, and the particular interests of their constituents, as fully accredited members of a committee. That is where the basic injustice originates. Forty per cent of the Members of this Progressive Conservative Party will not be officially represented on committee, and 1 might add that ten Members of the New Democratic Party, or one-third of their Members, will not be represented on the committee structures as presented here. But every backbench Liberal Member will have a job.
I am not saying this, Mr. Speaker, because I want another job, but I believe we have all come here as equals and we should be treated as such, in the spirit of the words of the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid), whose judgment and sensitivity to this problem I am sure we all appreciated this afternoon. Nevertheless, there seems to be a degree of hypocrisy in his suggestion that what we are achieving today is to give more power to the backbenchers, to improve the lot of private Members, as he put it. It is a matter of status, of pride, to be able to take a position as a member of a Parliamentary Standing Committee, he told us. Yet where is the status if every Liberal Member is able to enjoy one of those positions? Where is the pride for the 37 Members of the Conservative Party, as pointed out by my colleague, the Hon. Member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid), who will be deprived of the right to represent one or more of their special interests as a regular member of a standing committee?
That basic injustice, Mr. Speaker, cannot be denied. The Liberal Party has 53 per cent of the seats in this House, and they are trying to take 60 per cent of the seats on the standing committees, and that is not fair. The Liberal Members have made a great to-do about the fact the chairman would probably not vote very often, but, Mr. Speaker, if that is the case, why does the chairman need to vote at all? Perhaps a compromise could have been worked out. If, with the ten-member committee, we withdrew the right of the chairman to vote-if that is what they are trying to tell us-then we would have one NDP Member, three Conservative Members, and five Liberal Members instead of six. The sixth Member would be a totally unbiased chairman selected from any of the three Parties. He would not be able to vote because there would be no need for deciding the vote. There would be nine voting Members on that committee and there would never be a need for a tiebreaking vote. So if this is the line Government Members are taking, that the chairman would really be unbiased and would rarely vote anyway, then why would they not agree to withdraw the right of that person to vote?

I think, Mr. Speaker, there are those basic injustices. The additional point I want to make is that one would have expected the Striking Committee to look at the possibility of introducing some flexibility as to having a ten-Member committee or 15-Member committee. I do not agree with the Flon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) who said we would have to have either 9 or 17. If we were willing to give or take, and allowed the NDP a little heavier representation on some committees and the Conservative Party on others, if we looked at the workload of many of these committees, we would find that we could justify 13 and 15-Member committees in cases where there are only 10. I think in particular of the Finance Committee or the Fisheries and Forestry Committee which encompasses the three different subjects of fisheries, forestry and environment. We have had a problem there with revolving membership because the Members interested in fisheries were very often not interested in the forestry questions, and Members interested in forestry were not always interested in environment. When we look at the Miscellaneous Estimates Committee, we see the travesty of a hodge-podge of different subject matters such as Stats Canada, CBC, official languages, science and technology, Canada Post, Department of Supply and Services, Treasury Board, Auditor General, PMO and the Privy Council Office. You cannot have three Members from this Party and one Member from the NDP developing expertise in all of those areas. In one particular case, Mr. Speaker, that being science and technology, many Members of this House feel there should be one ten-member committee exclusively dedicated to that field. That would ensure that science and technology, which is at the heart of Canada's future economic development, would receive much more than lip service in this House and in the work of committees.
What I am saying, Mr. Speaker, is that the Striking Committee could be much more innovative. They could have used the latitude between 10 and 15 Member committees to be more fair to the specific interests of backbenchers and the need of their constituents by ensuring that the committee workload would be relatively equally balanced. These larger committees could be given 15 Members or 13 Members. The committees which meet less frequently need only ten. But to see the rule applied that there shall be ten Member committees except for the Committee on Agriculture and the Committee on External Affairs and National Defence really hamstrings many Members of this Party and this Parliament who would like to have a more effective opportunity to engage in discussions and bring forward constituents' concerns before committees. I think of transport. This Party is going to have three representatives on the Transport Committee. We deal with surface transport, air transport, marine transport, and we deal with West Coast and East Coast issues, Great Lakes issues, aviation policy; in short, a wide spectrum of subject matter, and we are going to have three Members from this Party dealing with all those areas.
I think the Striking Committee should go back to the work table, with the encouragement of this House, and exercise a lot more ingenuity in adjusting these committees and even proposing to the Committee dealing with Parliamentary Reform that we restructure some of these committees, retitle them, and try to be much more fair in the balance we provide so that all Members of Parliament including the 37 Members of this Party, will have an opportunity to participate as full, regular Members in the standing committees of this House.
